record.title: Creating an Emergency Water Supply
record.finding: At least one gallon/person/day for three days, aiming for two weeks, is a planning baseline. Suitable containers, cleaning, labels, cool storage and rotation are separate requirements; not a medical ration or universal survival clock.

record.title: Making Water Safe in an Emergency
record.finding: Use the applicable boiling or disinfectant instructions and local advisories. Fuel/toxic chemicals/radioactive contamination is not removed by boiling or ordinary disinfection. The book’s unspecified drops and universal illness-prevention claim are insufficient.

record.title: Water Disinfection for Travelers
record.finding: Silver products have limited US stored-water use; this does not validate jewelry as a disinfectant. Low-dose hydrogen peroxide lacks sufficient field disinfection evidence. Iodine has duration/thyroid/pregnancy cautions.

record.title: Rainwater and Your Health
record.finding: Air and collection materials can contaminate rainwater. Intended use, testing, treatment and separation from potable plumbing matter.

record.title: Home Water Treatment Systems
record.finding: Match treatment to actual germs/chemicals and product performance. Clear, cool, odorless water and a general treatment name do not prove potability.

record.title: Jerky
record.finding: Meat drying needs defined handling, preparation and heating controls. Elapsed low-heat drying and crispness alone do not validate a high-fat pemmican recipe or multi-year shelf life.

record.title: Ensuring Safe Canned Foods
record.finding: Use tested food-specific acidity/thermal processes, with pressure processing for low-acid foods. A jar seal, salting or time in a basement does not establish safety.

record.title: Pickled Eggs
record.finding: Published pickled-egg recipes require refrigeration and controlled vinegar formulations. There are no home-canning directions; the book’s generic salt-water treatment is not validated.

record.title: Food Safety After Emergencies
record.finding: Use actual appliance/food temperatures and time history. A cool cellar is not automatically adequate refrigeration for dairy or meats.

record.title: Candle Fire Safety
record.finding: Prefer flashlights during power outages; lit candles need stable holders, clearance and supervision. Household improvised candles/heaters are not certified by the general guidance.

record.title: Carbon Monoxide Poisoning Basics
record.finding: Never burn charcoal or use portable gas camp stoves indoors; use proper venting and CO alarms. An open window and wafting visible smoke do not establish protection from CO.

record.title: Wood-Burning Installation and Maintenance
record.finding: Professional installation/inspection, appropriate clearances, floor protection and vent configuration matter. This is historic Burn Wise program content, no longer updated as a program since2025; not a current local code determination.

record.title: Felling Hinge
record.locator: Logging eTool; good practices distinguished from standards
record.finding: Retained hinge wood guides the falling tree; cutting completely through it defeats that function. This limited engineering correction does not qualify a reader to fell trees.

record.title: Mushroom Hunting
record.finding: Positive species identification is necessary. Taste and other folk tests do not distinguish poisonous mushrooms; pleasant-tasting species may be toxic. This is mushroom-specific, not a complete edible-plant guide.

record.publisher: London and South East Burn Network / NHS
record.title: Minor Burn First Aid
record.finding: Use appropriate cooling and assessment; do not put toothpaste, butter or oils on burns. This does not validate the book’s egg/linseed/honey salve.

record.title: Cuts and Grazes
record.finding: Clean small wounds with suitable water and cover appropriately; serious/infected wounds need professional care. Household salt/vinegar/liquor is not established as a substitute or instrument-sterilization method.

record.title: Cleaning and Disinfecting Your Home
record.finding: Cleaning, sanitizing and disinfecting differ. Use appropriate products and label contact/dilution instructions. An untested vinegar/baking-soda spray is not a validated food-contact sanitizer.

record.title: Toothpastes
record.finding: Fluoride is required for accepted anticaries claims, and efficacy/safety data matter. A homemade abrasive paste is not equivalent to a tested fluoride dentifrice.

record.title: Preventing Mosquito and Tick Bites
record.finding: Mosquitoes can bite day and night. Screens, reducing standing water and EPA-registered repellents used as directed reduce exposure; bed nets alone do not establish complete protection.

record.title: Shellfish Safety FAQs
record.finding: Check current classified harvest waters/closures and VMRC requirements. Condemned shellfish waters are closed to private as well as commercial harvest; cool or clear-looking water is not approval.

record.title: Food Poisoning from Marine Toxins
record.finding: Shellfish can contain marine biotoxins before spoilage; immediate eating or cooking/salting does not remove those toxins. Source and harvest assessment remain necessary.

record.title: 12VAC5-610-980: Privy Types
record.finding: Privies have siting, construction, permitted-use and other wastewater requirements. A fixed100-yard distance and one-foot pit depth do not establish an approved waste-disposal plan at a sewered home.

record.title: Furbearer Trapping Regulations
record.finding: Deadfall traps are prohibited; other methods have species/season/license/property/check requirements. An outage does not establish an exemption.

record.title: Nongame Fishing Regulations
record.finding: Species, water, gear, limits and licenses apply; freshwater mussel possession is prohibited. A net across any stream or indiscriminate shellfish collection is not generally authorized.

record.title: Home Storage of Fruits and Vegetables in Root Cellars
record.finding: Crop temperature/humidity and ethylene compatibility differ. Examples include lower humidity for squash/pumpkins than many roots; no common90–95%RH requirement or universal storage period.

record.title: Root Crops
record.finding: Crop-specific hardiness, maturity, harvest and storage instructions differ; blanket early carrot harvest and all-root handling are not a complete local calendar.

record.title: Food Storage Conditions
record.finding: Humidity can damage dry foods and packaging; cool dry storage is distinct from humid produce storage. A cellar label does not establish safe food temperature or package performance.

record.title: Micro-hydro Systems
record.locator: Primary indexed excerpt only; direct access blocked
record.finding: Primary indexed excerpt states that available energy depends on flow and head. Direct page retrieval returned403; no detailed construction guidance or measured site power was established.

record.title: Topic420: Bartering Income
record.finding: Barter may create taxable income at fair market value; informal noncommercial exchange of similar services is distinguished. No cash does not necessarily mean no record or tax obligation.

record.title: Well Water Testing
record.finding: Use certified-laboratory testing and local interpretation. Annual indicators and local/event hazards matter; neither a dug well nor the existing irrigation well is assigned potable capacity.

record.title: 12VAC5-630-410: Well Construction
record.finding: Well class, geology, siting, casing and sanitary construction apply. A multi-year well supply is not established by digging alone.

record.title: Composting at Home
record.finding: Appropriate inputs, moisture and oxygen support composting; ordinary household compost is not a validated enclosed-room heating or waste-treatment system.

record.title: Thirty days is source organization
record.guidance: The daily sequence is a source format, not a recommended response timetable. Prepare and practice feasible skills beforehand; no evidence establishes automatic self-sufficiency by Day30 or indefinitely collapsed services.

record.title: Water doses and sources
record.guidance: Use the current source-/contaminant-specific official method. Few drops without volume, concentration and contact time, silver jewelry, oxygenation and dilute peroxide are not established water-safety procedures. Clear, cool or odorless water can still be unsafe.

record.title: Water storage and plumbing
record.guidance: Keep drinking water in suitable sanitized containers, label/date/rotate and protect it from contamination. A bathtub is not automatically a potable container. Follow utility advisories and safe plumbing instructions; draining household pipes is not a universal contamination-control process.

record.title: Waste disposal
record.guidance: Use a lawful locally suitable sewage/trash fallback, including safe containment and approved disposal. The one-foot pit/100-yard prescription and daily burning/burying are not a complete compliant method; protect groundwater and avoid indoor/open-burning hazards.

record.title: Pemmican preservation
record.guidance: No validated internal meat heat/drying endpoint, water activity, fat stability or packaging study supports this formula’s years-long shelf life.15hours/crispness and rendered-fat mixing temperature do not replace a safe process.

record.title: Smokehouse and shelf life
record.guidance: A building and up-to24hours smoke do not establish safe curing, heating, drying or storage for meat, fish, cheese and vegetables. The source does say cook smoked meat before eating; that does not validate interim storage.

record.title: Stove, chimney and combustion
record.guidance: Use properly designed/installed appliances and venting with approved clearances, supports and floor protection. A pipe through wood/flashing at a window, quarter-inch slope and improvised metal firebox are not a complete safe design. An open window does not make indoor charcoal burning safe.

record.title: Tree felling
record.guidance: Do not follow the cut-through-hinge instruction or stand directly behind a falling tree. Training, tree hazards, hinge/retreat planning, safe tools and competent help are unresolved; standing dead trees can be especially hazardous. This review supplies no replacement felling procedure.

record.title: Ash lye and soap
record.guidance: Feather dissolution is not a measured alkali concentration. Ash-derived solution, generic fats and the stated ounces/pints cannot establish a safe stoichiometric recipe or finished free-alkali limit. No36-bar/month yield or bath-safe soap is verified.

record.title: Foraging and taste tests
record.guidance: Do not identify edible plants/fungi by a skin rub, tiny taste or short symptom-free wait. Positive species/part/stage identification, preparation and contamination/legal checks are needed. A fixed100feet and one-third harvest rule are not universal guarantees.

record.title: Candles and improvised heaters
record.guidance: Prefer battery lighting. Food/crayon candles, nested pots and hot bricks have unassessed fire, burns, stability and exposure hazards. A second pot redistributes/stores heat rather than creating extra fuel energy; no room-heating capacity is demonstrated.

record.title: Trapping and hazardous pits
record.guidance: Confirm lawful species, method, land permission and checks. Virginia forbids deadfalls. Concealed sharp pits and perimeter injury hazards are retained only as excluded high-level references, without construction instructions or task mapping.

record.title: Cash and barter
record.guidance: Do not liquidate all cash from an unsupported prediction it becomes worthless. Compare essential needs and safe exchange options, maintain records and consider actual tax/legal obligations. No guaranteed crisis price or market exists.

record.title: Salt/brine is not universal preservation
record.guidance: The same undefined salt/sugar cure or two-tablespoon-per-quart brine does not validate meat, fish, poultry, eggs and cucumbers. Exact food-specific formulation, acidity/fermentation/thermal and temperature controls are needed; a month in a basement is no universal safety endpoint.

record.title: Open-fire cooking
record.guidance: Never rely on an open window/visible smoke removal as CO protection. Do not use volatile fuels or aerosol jets as fire starters. Cook using suitable equipment, heat/food-temperature controls and actual local fire restrictions. No nested-pot oven or hanging-meat method is validated.

record.title: Home remedies and first aid
record.guidance: Kitchen staples, liquor and herbs are not automatically suitable for wounds, sterile instruments or disease treatment. No egg/honey/linseed burn salve, salt/lard poultice, cough syrup or undosed tea is clinically approved here; obtain appropriate care and avoid delayed treatment.

record.title: Garden output and calendar
record.guidance: A watered newly planted plot does not guarantee continual food with little labor. Match actual climate, soil, seed/cutting, spacing, nutrients, pests and season; netting does not stop every pest. No household yield or calorie budget supplied.

record.title: Fish and shellfish
record.guidance: Limpets/mussels are mollusks, not crustaceans. Choose lawful safe harvest areas/species and maintain safe cold-chain/cooking practices. Marine biotoxins can be present before spoilage and survive cooking; immediate eating is not a safety test.

record.title: Disease and sanitation
record.guidance: Mosquitoes can bite day and night. Use appropriate bite prevention and hygiene; vinegar/baking soda is not validated sanitizing. Serious illness requires medical/public-health advice, and cause-specific precautions rather than isolating every illness identically. Cold/damp exposure is not itself a complete infectious-disease explanation.

record.title: Toothpaste on burns
record.guidance: Do not put toothpaste on burns. Follow appropriate cooling/covering and assessment; significant burns need medical attention.

record.title: Insulation and structural loads
record.guidance: Preserve appliance clearances, ventilation, safe exits and roof/attic loading. Do not pile furniture or pallets onto an unassessed structure or use random combustible packing as building insulation. Foil’s performance depends on configuration; a hand fan needs guards and safe mechanics.

record.title: Root-cellar conditions
record.guidance: Treat all four cellar sections as research only; construction remains deferred. Measure conditions and match crops, packaging and ethylene compatibility. No cave/trench/closet automatically functions as a refrigerator, and not all foods need90–95%RH.

record.title: Enclosed cellar heat
record.guidance: Do not use decomposing manure, improvised candles or unsuitable propane heaters as indoor humidity/temperature control. Pathogens, combustion, gases, ventilation and fire controls are unresolved; manure heat is not a safe cellar design.

record.title: Dental substitutions
record.guidance: Baking powder is not interchangeable with baking soda; an untested abrasive paste lacks fluoride anticaries equivalence. Garlic/onion, undosed clove oil, liquor and unspecified peroxide do not cure dental infection. Seek dental assessment; no extraction or anesthetic protocol supplied.

record.title: Brewing and missing distillation
record.guidance: The chapter title includes distilling but the body gives only an incomplete beer outline. Grain choice, mash/enzyme steps, cultured yeast, sanitation, safe fermentation and bottling endpoints are unresolved. No distillation procedure is present or invented.

record.title: Waterwheel power and machinery
record.guidance: Power is limited by actual flow/head, efficiency and seasonal availability. The sketch omits shaft/frame/gear loads, guarding, overspeed, electrical controls and permissions. No limitless/free/maintenance-light output or safe mill/saw is established.

record.title: Home security without injury traps
record.guidance: Use lawful noninjurious security, safe exits and emergency access. Cling film is not certified safety glazing; hidden pits, broken glass and rusty sharp barriers can injure family, visitors and responders and are not operational guidance.

record.title: Cellar dairy and food condition
record.guidance: Milk, some cheeses and meats need food-specific verified cold storage, not just a cool location. Do not cook visibly rotten food as a salvage rule. Match washing/trimming to the crop; projected use-by dates must not be invented from appearance.

record.title: Future capacity and property
record.guidance: Travel, livestock, fuel processing and water require skills, inputs, lawful access and a sustainable budget. Abandoned-looking resources are not necessarily ownerless. A future well is not automatically potable or reliable.

How to Outlive an EMP The Early Pioneer Way 
7 
Begin to ration food and  water, and consider how to deal 
with human waste, dirty water, and trash. If necessary, dig 
a pit at least 100 yards from the nearest food or water 
store and a minimum of one foot in d epth. Trash should 
be buried or burned on a daily schedule and moved away 
from your home to keep rats away. 
Secure your home before nightfall, checking the perimeter 
for breaches and ensuring that doors and windows are 
locked. Empty tin cans on a string are a simple early 
warning system for intruders, and broken glass can act as 
a barrier to entry. 
Immediately secure all the water in your home, filling 
bathtubs and any other container with the remaining 
water via the municipal supply, within pipes, and from 
storage and rainwater tanks . To flush pipes, turn off the 
water at the  shutoff valve, put a container under the 
lowest faucet in the house , and then open the lowest 
faucet and then a second faucet higher up.

How to Outlive an EMP The Early Pioneer Way 
8 
Your supplies of fresh meat will spoil quickly 
without refrigeration, but if turned into pem mican, 
it can last for years if stored away from moisture, 
heat, and direct sunlight. 
You will need equal portions of dried red meat and 
fat, preferably fat from red meat like beef tallow. You 
can also add dried berries to the mixture but no 
more than 5% of the total. 
Firstly, you will need to render the fat to boil off the 
water. Cut it up into small , half-inch chunks. Put the 
fat in a pot so it is about ¾ full, and put it on an open 
fire or a gas stove if you have one. Leave the lid off , 
and place a thermometer in the pot.

How to Outlive an EMP The Early Pioneer Way 
9 
Boil the fat for about an hour, being careful not to let 
the temperature exceed 250°F. Stir continually until 
the boiling stops and only small bubbles rise from 
the liquid fat. Next, strain the fat through a sieve.  
Secondly, dry out you r meat by shredding it then 
cooking it over low heat for about 15 hours, until it 
is crispy. You will need three times the amount of 
fresh meat as you need dried meat as it reduces to 
about 1/3 of its weight during drying. 
Finally, mix equal quantities of the dried meat and 
rendered fat together by heating up the  rendered fat 
until it liquefies (keeping the  temperature below 
150°F), and then stir in the meat until you have a 
mixture like brownies. 
To store the pemmican, press it into Ziploc bags and 
seal it up, making sure there are no air bubbles 
remaining. Protect the bags from light and moistu re 
by wrapping them in aluminum.

How to Outlive an EMP The Early Pioneer Way 
12 
Smoking your food can keep meat, fish, cheese , and 
vegetables fresh for months. 
First, lay down the base of the smokehouse using a 
layer of cinder blocks w ith their open ends pointing 
upright. Size the smokehouse according to the 
blocks, wood, and bricks you have on hand—even a 
few square feet is workable. 
Second, add the frame using wooden strips or beams 
to construct the vertical and horizontal edges.  Bolt 
this in place over the base, and then use wooden 
planks to make the walls and roof. Cedar is the best 
wood as its natural oils will help preserve food.

source_components.source_label: Documentary page context; adjacent material may be included; image text is not transcribed here
source_components.text:
How to Outlive an EMP The Early Pioneer Way 
13 
Third, build a firebox from bricks and mortar. It is 
simply a box with one side open to add fuel. It should 
be smaller than the base of the smokehouse. You can 
either build it in the middle of the base and leave a 
hole open in the top of it for smoke to trickle out  of 
or build it next to the smokehouse and use a pipe to 
carry smoke from the top of the fireb ox to the 
smokehouse. 
By placing hooks on the ceiling, you can hang your 
food to smoke. Make sure there is enough space 
between things for the smoke to circulate; don’t pack 
it too tight. 
To start smoking, build a fire in the firebox using 
non-resinous, dry wood. The best choices are 
hickory, maple, pecan, oak, and mesquite. The wood 
must not be green or producing sap or resin , as this 
will ruin the food. Smoke your food for up to 24 
hours. Remember, you need to cook smoked meat 
before eating it.

How to Outlive an EMP The Early Pioneer Way 
14 
For most people, firewood is the only easily available 
heat source, so a properly installed wood -burning 
stove is essential. 
Your stove can be a ready -made unit, or you can 
improvise one with a large metal box into which you 
can add some bricks to even out the temperature 
inside. 
Position your stove in the middle of the room , if 
possible, and place it on a fireproof surface, such as 
bricks, ceramic tiles, or gravel. Make sure the surface 
extends a couple of feet farther than the stove to stop 
hot sparks.

How to Outlive an EMP The Early Pioneer Way 
15 
To avoid doing major building work, just run the 
chimney of the stove out of a window. Remove the 
glass pane, and replace it with aluminum flashing or 
a piece of wood; then cut a hole for the chimney pipe. 
Make sure you secure  the chimney and your 
improvised window to prevent wind damage. 
The most important factor in running your chimney 
is making sure there is an upward gradient of at least

How to Outlive an EMP The Early Pioneer Way 
18 
For washing clothes, bathing , and cleaning up, you 
need to secure an easily renewable supply of soap. 
Pioneer soap is a mixture of a fatty acid and an alkali 
with water. You can use any kind of fat, like lard or 
vegetable oil, and you will use lye as your alkali. 
To make the lye, put wood ashes into a pillowcase, 
and put this into a bucket. Pour on a gallon of boiling 
water, and work the pillowcase with a long wooden 
spoon, like making a giant cup of tea.  
Repeat this for an hour or two, and then test the lye 
by throwing a chicken feather into the bucket. If it 
dissolves, t he lye is the correct strength. T ake the 
resulting brown mixture , and boil off the water, or 
let it evaporate away slowly.

Plants absorb pollution , so avoid areas close to 
major roads and anywhere within 100 feet of a 
source of pollution —like a cesspit in a garden for 
example. You should also avoid spots where animals 
have left droppings and close to large buildings, car 
parks, and hospitals. 
A sharp knife is usually all you need to forage. If you 
want to return to forage from the same group of 
plants, take no more than 1/3 of each plant. 
Test your foraged food before eating it in quantity. 
Try a small piece first, and rub it on your skin. An 
allergic reaction, such as a rash or swelling, indicates 
it isn’t safe. Next, try eating a small piece, and wait a 
few hours. If you haven’t suffered an upset stomach, 
the plant is probably safe. 
Immediately after you return from foraging, either 
use what you have found or take steps to keep it 
fresh.

How to Outlive an EMP The Early Pioneer Way 
28 
Salting is the easiest way to keep food fresh for long 
periods without needing heat or equipment to do the 
job. It’s an ancient preservation technique. 
To cure meat or fish with ordinary salt, cut it into 
slices, and cover it with a mixture of salt and a little 
brown sugar, honey, or maple syrup. Pack the slices 
tightly together in an airtight jar, packing all the way 
up to the rim. 
You can also use brine —water mixed with salt —to 
pickle things like cucumber s, eggs, or chunks of fish 
and chicken. Mix up a strong brine solu tion, roughly 
two tablespoons of salt per quart of water. Next , cut 
up the food you want to pickle into small chunks, and 
add it to the solution.

How to Outlive an EMP The Early Pioneer Way 
29 
Pickled food is best stored in clean jars with tight lids 
to k eep out air. Steriliz e the jars before pouring i n 
the solution by swilling them out with boiling water 
or wiping the insides with a little bleach and a rag 
then rinsing. Find a cold place, perhaps in a 
basement, to store the pickled and cured foods. After 
about a month, they should be fully preserved. 
Potatoes just need to be stored with straw to 
preserve them for many months. Line a wooden box 
with straw, and then fill it about a foot in depth with 
potatoes. Add another thick layer of straw , and then 
add more potatoes until the box is full. Cover the box 
with a strong, rat-proof lid, and store the box. 
When cooking with salted foods, test a small piece to 
see if the salt is overpoweringly strong. If it is, simply 
soak the food in clean water overnight , and then 
rinse to reduce the salt levels.

How to Outlive an EMP The Early Pioneer Way 
30 
The lack of fuel and electricity and the difficulty of 
using even off -grid technology to produce enough 
heat for cooking means you’ll be using an open fire 
to cook on a daily basis. 
Building an open fire is easy, whether you’re us ing 
logs and kindling wood or coal/charcoal and balled 
up newspaper. Make loose layers in a pyramid 
shape, and don’t pack things too tightly so that 
oxygen can circulate as it burns. 
If you are cooking or heating inside, especially when 
burning coal, you m ust let the smoke escape or you 
run the risk of carbon monoxide poisoning. At a 
minimum, leave the window open , and waft the 
smoke out.

32 
Pioneers knew how to turn simple kitchen staples, 
herbs, and natural ingredients into essential first aid 
supplies. 
Many items are effective just as they are. Vinegar is 
good for cleaning wounds as is salt, although both 
will sting. Milk or toni c water deals with acid reflux 
or an upset stomach, and alcohol, especially white -
colored liquor , is good for disinfecting, pain relief , 
and sterilizing things like tweezers or blades when 
removing thorns.  
Pioneers were also good at making simple 
medicines. Make a salve for burns and insect stings 
by mixing one part honey, two parts linseed oil, and 
an egg yolk.

important to use passive methods to keep your

adding extra layers of insulation over windo ws. 
Towels and old clothing are great for trapping heat, 
and reflective aluminum foil is also a fine insulator. 
Check your home for any draughts or gaps where 
cold air can get in ; ill-fitting doors are a common 
culprit. Fill gaps with balled up newspaper. You can 
also double up on carpets and rugs —the more 
layers, the better you will trap heat.

circulate by leaving vents open.

source_components.text:
How to Outlive an EMP The Early Pioneer Way 
65 
Your long -term thinking involves going from , say, 
collecting rain water to digging a well to provide 
water for years rather than a few days at a t ime. In 
the same way, keeping animals like chickens or goats 
will give you milk, eggs , and meat for years rather 
than the few small animals you could trap. 
You should also plan ways to save time and effort. In 
a survival situation , it is easy to become so trapped 
by day -to-day chores that no long -term 
improvements are possible. To break the cycle, think 
smart. For example, instead of collecting firewood 
for a week, plan ahead , and cut and store the whole 
winter’s firewood in one operation. This kind of 
aggregating is more time efficient than lots of little 
tasks. 
Above all, assume that the disordered post EMP 
world will last indefinitely, and stay positive.
